back: The rigid outer shell of the Earth (crust plus uppermost mantle), broken into tectonic plates.
A weak, partly molten layer of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere that flows very slowly.
Oceanic: thin (about 5-10 km), dense, young basalt. Continental: thick (about 25-70 km), less dense, often very old.
Outer core: liquid iron and nickel (magnetic field). Inner core: solid iron and nickel, kept solid by enormous pressure.
Wegener's theory that the continents were once joined in Pangaea and have drifted apart.
Jigsaw fit, matching fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), matching rocks and mountains, past climates (glacial traces in southern Africa, coal in Antarctica).
Mantle convection currents, ridge push (cooling lithosphere slides from ridges) and slab pull (sinking slabs drag plates).
Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.
About 1-10 cm a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow.
